newsitem.title: USA: Second World Trade Center bombing trial opens.
newsitem.headline: Second World Trade Center bombing trial opens.

text.p: A U.S. prosecutor charged on Tuesday that the alleged mastermind of the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing and his co-defendant were "self-proclaimed terrorists" who had wanted to kill thousands of people.

Opening his argument in the second trial for the deadly blast at the 110-floor twin towers, prosecutor Lev Dassin pointed his finger at Ramzi Yousef and said: "This man, one of the masterminds to the bomb, ordered, mixed, stored chemicals" and planted the bomb that killed six people on Feb. 26, 1993.

"This self-proclaimed army of terrorists was like no other," said Dassin, an assistant U.S. attorney. "They were sending a message to Americans that this could happen to anyone, at any time ... and that anyone can be a victim of a savage attack on American soil."

Yousef, who claims Palestinian and Pakistani ancestry, was indicted in 1993 on charges of taking part in the bombing, along with four Moslem fundamentalists who were convicted in 1994. The four were each sentenced to 240 years in prison for their roles in the blast.
His co-defendant Eyad Ismoil, a Jordanian, is accused of driving the van that carried the bomb into the basement garage of the huge complex.
Yousef and Ismoil fled the country the night of the explosion. Yousef was captured in Pakistan in 1995 and Ismoil was arrested in Jordan last year.

Dassin said that after his capture, Yousef "bragged about the bombing and said he had wanted to topple one of the towers into the other, killing thousands of people ... sending a message to Americans that they were at war."
He said Yousef and Ismoil were "self-proclaimed terrorists" who wanted to retaliate "in return for the U.S. government's support of Israel."
The defendants' lawyers did not outline their case to the jury in Manhattan federal court but instead focused on reminding them to "keep an open mind" throughout the trial.
Yousef's attorney, Roy Kulcsar, urged jurors not to allow "the emotion and distress" of seeing grisly photos of the six victims "affect your decision."
If convicted, both men face a possible maximum term of life in prison.
The trial began after a day's delay over problems with jurors and less than a week after authorities said they had prevented a suicide bombing attack on the New York subway by Middle Eastern men.
In interviews, jurors convinced Judge Kevin Duffy they had not been prejudiced by the alleged subway plot or last Wednesday's bombing of a Jerusalem market by Palestinian militants.
Officials say there is no apparent link between two men arrested and accused of planning an attack on the subway and Yousef.

But the New York Post and ABC News have quoted unidentified investigators as saying one of the suspects left a note demanding the release of Yousef. FBI and New York police officials declined to comment on the reports.

The trial's first witness, Charles Maikish, former director of the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey's World Trade Department, said he was sitting at his desk on the 35th floor when he "felt the tower heave."
He described the damage to the building's systems, including the communication and fire detection systems that were blown out in the explosion.

Security at the courthouse was tight as bomb-sniffing dogs checked every room inside and every person entering the building. Metal detectors were used to examine the personal belongings of those attending the trial.

The 1,200 pound (544 kg) urea nitrate bomb killed six and injured more than 1,000. It devastated the underground garage of the complex, forced a shutdown of all electric power and sent thick black smoke pouring through the twin towers.

The prosecutor said Yousef ordered 1,000 pounds (454 kgs) of urea and 100 gallons (378.5 litres) of nitric acid which he said when mixed together "makes a powerful explosion." He said Yousef later ordered hydrogen "which gave the bomb an extra kick."
Dassin said the two men took a rented yellow Ryder van into the B-2 level of the public parking area and "at 12:18 p.m. EST, the bomb exploded, killing six people these men did not even know."
